metadata.title: Classroom emotions in civic education: A multilevel approach to antecedents and effects

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used an online questionnaire and a political knowledge test administered to students in Austrian vocational schools. Schools were selected using a random sample of all schools in three Austrian regions, stratified by region, and data collection occurred during regular lessons in summer terms 2021 and 2022. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, weighting variables are not documented for the analytic models. Missing data were handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) within the multilevel SEM framework rather than through weight-based adjustments.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs); instead, it models latent variables from questionnaire scales (open classroom climate and discrete emotions) and uses a political knowledge test scored from correct/incorrect items. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. Missing data are addressed with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in the multilevel SEM, which is a model-based approach rather than PV-based multiple imputation; the paper reports FIML and excludes only cases missing all variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 1162 students from 19 Austrian vocational schools and 89 classes. From 1321 students who initially started the questionnaire, 159 (12%) were excluded based on pre-registered criteria: high completion speed and self-reported dishonesty. The study used multilevel SEM with students nested in classes; missing data were handled with FIML, excluding only participants with missing values on all variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS-based open classroom climate (ICCS 2016 scale adaptation) in Austrian vocational schools (2021-2022), multilevel within-class and between-class
top_predictors: Open classroom climate (relative to class mean)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Bayesian estimator). Explained variance (R²): open classroom climate → enjoyment (within R²w=0.086; between R²b=0.840); open classroom climate → anxiety (within R²w=0.076; between R²b=0.025) and boredom (within R²w=0.067; between R²b=0.367); emotions → political knowledge (within R²w: enjoyment=0.147; shame=0.197; anxiety=0.211; boredom=0.159). Indirect effects via emotions not supported (Table 6).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS-based open classroom climate scale adaptation in Austrian vocational schools (2021-2022) the study leveraged open classroom climate and discrete emotions (enjoyment, shame, anxiety, boredom) to model political knowledge, finding that open classroom climate predicted enjoyment and (at least at the within level) anxiety and boredom, while all four emotions showed significant within-level associations with political knowledge (enjoyment positive; shame/anxiety/boredom negative). This indicates that improving the emotional experience during civic discussions—especially increasing enjoyment and reducing anxiety/boredom—may be more actionable for political knowledge gains than changing openness alone, though the study is observational and multilevel measurement fit at the between level was limited.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS-based open classroom climate (ICCS 2016 scale adaptation) in Austrian vocational schools (2021-2022), multilevel within-class and between-class
top_predictors: Open classroom climate (relative to class mean)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Bayesian estimator). Explained variance (R²) for indirect effects (within level): enjoyment indirect effect R²w=0.266; anxiety indirect effect R²w=0.133. Direct within-level associations reported via mediation paths: enjoyment, anxiety, and shame positively related to participation (relative to class mean), while boredom negatively related (within R²w: shame=0.129; boredom=0.136). Indirect effects (Table 8, within): enjoyment β=0.137, 95% CI [0.069, 0.228]; shame β=-0.038, 95% CI [-0.100, 0.012]; anxiety β=-0.068, 95% CI [-0.140, -0.016]; boredom β=0.029, 95% CI [-0.025, 0.091].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS-based open classroom climate scale adaptation in Austrian vocational schools (2021-2022) the study leveraged open classroom climate and discrete emotions (enjoyment, shame, anxiety, boredom) to model intention to political participation, finding that openness was indirectly associated with participation through enjoyment at the student (within-class) level, while anxiety showed a competitive mediation pattern (openness reduced anxiety, and anxiety was positively associated with participation). This indicates that civic-education practice should prioritize creating an open, supportive discussion climate that fosters enjoyment and manages anxiety to strengthen students’ future political engagement, while recognizing that causal effects cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional observational design.

data.outcome_summary: This study used Austrian vocational-school survey data collected in 2021–2022 (N=1162 students; 19 schools; 89 classes) to test how an open classroom climate (measured with an ICCS 2016-based scale adaptation) relates to discrete classroom emotions (enjoyment, shame, anxiety, boredom) and how these emotions relate to political knowledge and intended political participation. The authors estimated multilevel SEM with doubly-latent mediation and random slopes, using Bayesian estimation and reporting explained variance (R²) and indirect effects with credible intervals. They found that open classroom climate predicted enjoyment at both within- and between-class levels and predicted anxiety and boredom at the within level (and boredom also at the between level). Emotions were significant predictors of political knowledge (within R²w: enjoyment=0.147; shame=0.197; anxiety=0.211; boredom=0.159), but mediation via emotions was not supported for knowledge. For participation, enjoyment showed a significant positive indirect effect (within β=0.137, CI [0.069, 0.228]), while anxiety showed a significant negative indirect effect (within β=-0.068, CI [-0.140, -0.016]) consistent with competitive mediation. Limitations include cross-sectional observational data and weaker between-level model fit for some outcomes.
